claims.why_uncovered: The rule applies whenever there was a traditional IRA contribution and either spouse was covered by a retirement plan, even if the contributor was not the covered person. The encoded question asks whether the filer or spouse 'put money into a traditional IRA for 2025 while covered by a retirement plan', which ties coverage to the contributor. So a filer who contributed while only the spouse was covered (including a married-filing-separately filer whose spouse is covered) could answer No. That filer is not routed to Pub. 590-A. ssb.ira_line20 then figures the IRA deduction as if no one were covered, and that feeds worksheet line 6.

claims.quote: * This column must also be used by a qualifying surviving spouse.
claims.why_uncovered: table_tax cites only the table's row and column headings ("If line 15 (taxable income) is—", "And you are—", "Your tax is—"). The status input is bound to the Form 1040 filing status, which can be qualifying surviving spouse. The Tax Table has no qualifying surviving spouse column. Nothing in the encoding cites or implements the footnote that sends a qualifying surviving spouse to the married filing jointly column. The f1040 qualifying surviving spouse refusal fires only when the tests are not met. It does not cover a valid qualifying surviving spouse looking up tax. So nothing shows the table lookup is correct for that status.

claims.why_uncovered: Column 1(b) can be either the tips the employer reported on Form W-2 or the tips the filer reported to the employer on Forms 4070 (or a similar monthly report). The question for tipjob.tips offers only W-2 box 7, box 14 or a separate employer statement. Nothing asks for or allows the Form 4070 total. The instructions say that total may be more accurate, and so larger, when box 1 or box 5 is more than the $176,100 social security wage base. The label of tipjob.amount names Forms 4070, but its only input is tipjob.tips, which never asks for that amount.

claims.why_uncovered: u1250.line10 restates only the worksheet's line text. It drops the 'See instructions' rules that fix the amount: the deemed fully taxable transfer, and the proportionate reduction when only part of the realized gain is recognized. No question asks about these, and no refusal covers them. Nothing in the encoding asks for or flags the required attachment under Regulations section 1.1(h)-1(e).

claims.quote: You can elect to include your nontaxable combat pay in earned income when figuring your exclusion or deduction, even if you elect not to include it in earned income for the EIC or the credit for child and dependent care expenses. / To make the election, include all of your nontaxable combat pay in the amount you enter on line 18 (line 19 for your spouse if filing jointly). / If you are filing jointly and both you and your spouse received nontaxable combat pay, you can each make your own election. / The amount of your nontaxable combat pay should be shown in box 12 of your Form(s) W-2 with code Q.
claims.why_uncovered: The encoding takes dependent care benefits from box 10 for Form 2441 Part III. It never asks for box 12 code Q nontaxable combat pay or for the filer's election to include it in earned income on lines 18 and 19. No refusal covers combat pay. The election can raise the earned-income limit and therefore the excludable dependent care benefits.
